**On Budget Management:**
When I make a bid, I need to track my actual remaining budget correctly. The record shows I stated [budget: 84] after bidding 16 with a starting budget of 30—this is impossible and indicates I lost track of my finances mid-game. Before each bid, I will mentally verify: starting budget minus all previous winning bids equals my current available funds.

**On Opening Bids:**
When a lot opens with no standing bid, I will not default to a minimal opening bid just to conserve resources. If a lot is worth significantly more to me than the estimate, I will open more aggressively to discourage participation. A lot worth 44 with an estimate of 32 warrants a stronger opening than 10.

**On Value-to-Price Ratio:**
When the standing bid is well below a lot's value to me, I will bid to win it. If a lot is worth 54 and the standing bid is 8, the margin is strong enough to justify winning.

**On Passing:**
When a lot's value to me is below the estimate or the current bid is already close to its value, I will pass. A lot worth 17 with an estimate of 21 and an existing bid of 4 is not worth pursuing—I correctly passed on this.

**On Final Round Discipline:**
In the second round of any lot, I will not automatically escalate. When I'm outbid in a final round and my remaining budget is limited, I need to accept that I may not win every valuable lot. I should only raise if the margin between value and current price still justifies the bid.

**On Competitive Tracking:**
I will track what my opponents have won and their likely scores so I can gauge whether I'm ahead or behind. This helps me decide when to fight for a lot and when to conserve budget for remaining opportunities.

**The mistake I made:** I finished with only +39 points by winning one lot. I need to win more lots. Passing on value is the safer error—I should bid more aggressively when a lot's value to me exceeds its current price, especially early in the auction when I have full budget.

# Playbook for ref_auction

When I see a lot where the value to me significantly exceeds the current bid, I bid immediately rather than waiting—the margin of safety is what matters.

When opening a lot with no bids yet, I open at the minimum raise to secure it cheaply and preserve budget for future lots.

When deciding whether to raise in round 2 of any lot, I compare the minimum raise price against the lot's value to me. If that price is still well below value, I bid it.

I track my wins relative to other bidders, but I don't let that override value calculations. I bid when value is present, not based on keeping score even.

I remember that my budget statement matters—I must always include both the bid amount and my remaining budget in my reply, and I need to track my remaining budget accurately across all my decisions.

When it's the final lot and final round, I bid if value is present, since this is my last opportunity and there are no future lots to preserve budget for.

I avoid overbidding in early rounds just to win something. Instead, I identify lots with the strongest value-to-estimate ratios and compete for those.

When the standing bid is low relative to value, I don't assume others will bid me up to the true value—I bid what makes sense for me based on my own valuation, not predictions about other bidders.

I should have bid more aggressively on high-value lots in middle rounds rather than opening minimally. Opening too low sometimes means I win at a good price, but it can also mean I lose to competitors who bid higher. I need to balance getting good value against actually winning the lots I target.

# My Auction Playbook

**On valuation and bidding discipline:**
When a lot's value to me exceeds the current bid, I will bid. The margin between my private valuation and the standing bid is what matters, not the estimate.

When I'm in round 1 of 2, I will bid conservatively to preserve capital for round 2 and remaining lots, even when I have strong value. A minimum or near-minimum raise is appropriate.

When I'm in round 2 of 2 (the final round for that lot), I can bid more aggressively since there are no more opportunities to contest that lot.

**On calculating profit potential:**
Before bidding, I will quickly estimate: value to me minus potential bid price. If this margin is positive, the bid is justified. I will not overthink the estimate price—my private valuation is what drives my decisions.

**On budget management:**
I will track my remaining budget carefully after each win. I should expect to spend roughly 40-50% of my total budget per episode and adjust my aggression accordingly as the auction progresses.

I will not assume I have more budget than I actually do. When calculating whether to bid, I will base my decision on my actual remaining funds, not theoretical starting amounts.

**What didn't work:**
My budget tracking was inconsistent—I stated "budget: 78" in round 2 after spending 22, but this was mathematically wrong (should have been around 56-58 depending on starting amount). This confusion didn't stop me from bidding, but it shows I need to track more carefully.

I was uncertain about when to be aggressive versus conservative. I should commit to the principle: cautious in round 1, aggressive in round 2.
